name: measured-proven
title: Measured: fires on AI prose
description: Rules that fired on AI prose and either never touched a human document or hit AI at least three times as often. Grouped by how they behaved, not by where they came from, so the source of each is recorded in its "from" field. Generated by tools/group-by-evidence.mjs against the corpus described in research/audit.md; re-run it when the corpus grows.

rules.name: “No X, no Y” chains
rules.description: Two or more “no …” items in a row, e.g. “No fluff, no filler, no jargon.” The badge counts the “no” items.
rules.suggest: Say what it does have. A denial chain lists absences instead of substance.

hit: No sign-ups, no downloads, no hassle — just paste and go.
The plan has no hidden fees and no long-term contracts.
No fluff, no filler, no jargon, no corporate buzzwords.
It ships with no bells and whistles, no fluff.
NO FEES, NO CONTRACTS, NO SURPRISES
no fluff; no filler
no time, no money, no way to say no thanks
no-code, no-fuss setup

No fluff, no filler.
No ads here.
miss: There is no catch here, honestly.
No, no, I insist.
no no no
with no list patterns at all, so nothing lights up.
I know nothing, notice nothing.

rules.name: “The entire … is”
rules.description: “The entire point / game / business model is …” — the flipped twin of “is the entire”.
rules.suggest: Replace the totalising claim with the specific mechanism.

hit: The entire point is that nobody reads.
The entire business model is built on churn.
The entire point of the exercise is repetition.
The entire team was exhausted.
miss: He ate the entire pizza.
The entire history of the modern industrial world economy is complex.

rules.name: “Is real … and / not”
rules.description: “The X is real, and / not …”, including “is the real … and it”. Skips “real estate”, “real time”, and similar.
rules.suggest: Cut "is real". Give the evidence that makes it real.

hit: The improvement is real, and it's not subtle.

miss: He is a real estate agent and it shows.
Is it real? And does it matter?

rules.name: “Is the whole …”
rules.description: Any subject + “is the whole point / trick / pitch / idea”, plus the “here is the whole …” opener. The twin of “is the entire …”, and a generalisation of “That’s the whole …” to subjects other than that/this.
rules.suggest: Name the thing directly instead of gesturing at its totality.

hit: Distribution is the whole game.

miss: The whole team showed up.

rules.name: “That’s the part …”
rules.description: Gesturing at a favoured detail instead of stating it: “that is the part a counter can’t reach”, “the part that makes me trust the rest”, “my favourite part of …”.
rules.suggest: State the detail instead of pointing at it.

rules.name: Colon into a triple
rules.description: A colon opening onto three or more comma-separated prose items: “separate ports, processes, and local state”. The most common shape LLM prose uses to sound concrete. Tightened from upstream: items must read as prose, not as code, measurements or proper-noun lists.
rules.suggest: Fine in a real list. Suspect when it is prose padding out to three items.

rules.name: “Not X but Y” (unqualified)
rules.description: The negation flip without a just/only/merely qualifier: “not a tool but a partner”. Slop Score weights this construction at 25% of its entire score, on its own, separate from word lists.
rules.suggest: Say what it is. The negated half is usually a straw man nobody proposed.

hit: It is not a tool but a partner.
The problem is not about speed but about accuracy.
This was not the end but the beginning.
The fix came not from the compiler but from the linker.
miss: He did not know but she did.
I am not sure but I will check.
She did not buy the car but rented one instead.
We are not in a hurry but we should start soon.

rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 0 hits in 0/18 human documents, 4 in 3/18 AI documents.

rules.name: No parentheses at all
rules.description: The Economist found that models use “hardly any parentheses”. This fires only at zero, over a document long enough for zero to mean something.
rules.suggest: An aside in parentheses is among the cheapest ways to vary rhythm. A long document with none is unusual.

hit: The system reads the file. It parses each line into a record. The records go to a queue. A worker takes them off the queue. It validates them. Invalid records are logged and dropped. Valid records go to the database. The database applies them in order. Each batch is committed together. If a batch fails the whole batch is retried. After three failures the batch moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue every morning. Most entries turn out to be malformed input. They come from one upstream partner. We opened a ticket with them in March. The ticket is still open. We now reject their malformed records at the edge instead. That reduced the dead letter volume by ninety percent. The remaining failures are genuine bugs on our side. We fix them as they appear. The edge rejection was a fifteen line change. It shipped on a Tuesday afternoon. Nobody noticed it. The operator stopped getting paged at six in the morning. She sent a message to say so. That message is pinned in the channel. It is the only performance review that change will ever get. The queue has run clean for four months now. We have not touched the retry logic since. The dead letter queue holds eleven records. All eleven are from the same partner. We suspect a date parsing bug on their side. They have not replied to the ticket. We check the queue on Fridays now instead of daily. Nothing else has changed. The runbook still says to check daily. Someone should update it. Nobody has. The alert threshold is also stale. It was set for the old volume. We lowered it once and then forgot about it entirely.
miss: The system reads the file, one line at a time, and parses each line into a record. Records go to a queue, where a worker picks them up, validates them, and either drops them or writes them on. Invalid records are logged, dropped, and counted. Valid ones reach the database, which applies them in order, in batches, committing each batch together. If a batch fails, the whole batch is retried; after three failures it moves to a dead letter queue. An operator reviews that queue each morning, and most of what is in there, it turns out, is malformed input from a single upstream partner. We opened a ticket in March, which is still open, so we now reject their malformed records at the edge, which cut the dead letter volume by about ninety percent. What remains are genuine bugs, on our side, and we fix those as they appear. The edge rejection, when we finally wrote it, was fifteen lines. It shipped on a Tuesday, quietly, and nobody noticed except the operator (who stopped getting paged at six in the morning). She sent a message to say so, and that message, pinned in the channel ever since, is the only performance review the change will ever get. The queue has run clean for four months, and we have not touched the retry logic since. Eleven records sit in the dead letter queue, all from the same partner, and we suspect a date parsing bug on their side. They have not replied. We check on Fridays now, rather than daily, and nothing else has changed. The runbook, which still says daily, is stale; so is the alert threshold, set for the old volume, lowered once, and then forgotten about entirely by everyone involved.

rules.note: Zero is a deliberately literal reading of “hardly any”. It still fires on perfectly good human prose that simply never reaches for a parenthesis: one document in the 16-document corpus, about 6%.
rules.evidence: On the audit corpus: 6 hits in 6/18 human documents, 18 in 18/18 AI documents.

rules.name: Nominalisations pile up
rules.description: All four models the Economist tested favoured nominalisations: verbs turned into nouns, so that things are described rather than done. Counted per thousand words.
rules.suggest: Turn the nouns back into verbs. “The implementation of the validation” is “validating”.

rules.name: “genuinely”
rules.description: The intensifier models reach for to signal sincerity. Fifty-three times the human rate, and the highest-ratio tell measured. Measured at ×53 vs humans.
rules.suggest: Delete it. If the claim needs the word, the claim is not carrying itself.

rules.name: “rather than”
rules.description: The 2026 flagship tell: models reach for “rather than” where humans write “instead of” or rephrase. Measured at ×5.0 vs humans.
rules.suggest: Write “instead of”, or rephrase so the contrast is not needed.
